source.title: BLUEFIN: Benchmarking LLM Agents on Financial Spreadsheets

issues.problem: "An audit of 50 operational spreadsheets found 117 errors, with impacts up to $100,000,000" — the document says this audit was by Powell et al. and the errors made up 0.8% to 1.8% of formula cells. The page omits the source, and the "As on the earlier page for this document" reminder adds nothing.
issues.suggestion: Attribute the audit to Powell et al. and trim the reminder to a clean one-line mention of programmatic verifiability, naming the earlier page.

issues.problem: The prompt asks "which rubric categories could catch this and how". The required criterion demands specifically that Perturbation is identified. A reader who answers Model Integration or Formula Correctness, which are defensible catches, could fail.
issues.suggestion: Make the prompt ask which category would catch it when an input changes, or make the required criterion accept any category that catches a hardcode with a valid reason.

issues.problem: "the paper reports no confidence intervals that I can see" and "the judge family (GPT) also competes as a tested model" are stated with more certainty than warranted. The model-family overlap is true (GPT-5.4 judge, GPT-5.5 tested), but the claim about the paper's missing statistics is an absence claim.
issues.suggestion: Hedge the claim, for example "as far as I can tell", and state that the judge and a tested model come from the same vendor family.

issues.problem: The scenario's phrasing "showed no benefit from the costliest model" is in the correct option. One case study shows Gemini matching Opus on one task, which is thin support for a general rule.
issues.suggestion: Reword the correct option to say that the case study found a cheaper model matched the costlier one on a routine wiring task.
